expectedText:
COVID-19 RIGHT OF RECALL FOR HOSPITALITY AND BUILDING-SERVICE WORKERS — INFORMATION SHEET AND NOTICE TEMPLATE
Prepared for Taylor Morgan · Bayview Grand Hotel, LLC

RIGHT-OF-RECALL NOTICE — IDENTIFICATION
RIGHT-OF-RECALL NOTICE UNDER CALIFORNIA LABOR CODE SECTION 2810.8

Employer / covered enterprise: Bayview Grand Hotel, LLC
Description of covered enterprise: 180-room hotel

Laid-off employee: Taylor Morgan
Employee's job classification at the time of separation: Banquet Server
Date of employee's most recent layoff / separation from active employment: April 15, 2020

Position now being offered: Banquet Server
Date of this written offer: September 6, 2026
Deadline to accept or decline this offer: September 15, 2026

This notice is provided in connection with California Labor Code Section 2810.8, which requires certain hotel, private club, event center, airport hospitality, airport service provider, and building-service employers to offer available positions to their own laid-off employees, in a specified order of preference, before hiring from outside that pool.

WHICH EMPLOYERS AND WHICH WORKERS THE STATUTE COVERS
Labor Code Section 2810.8 does not apply to employers generally. It reaches only an "enterprise," a term the statute defines to mean a hotel, private club, event center, airport hospitality operation, airport service provider, or the provision of building service to office, retail, or other commercial buildings, and "building service" is itself separately defined to mean janitorial, building maintenance, or security services. Within a covered enterprise, the statute's protections run only to a "laid-off employee": an employee who worked for the employer for six months or more and whose most recent separation from active employment occurred on or after March 4, 2020 for a reason related to the COVID-19 pandemic, such as a public health directive, government shutdown order, lack of business, a reduction in force, or another economic, nondisciplinary reason. The statute builds in a rebuttable presumption favoring coverage: a separation attributed to a lack of business, a reduction in force, or another economic, nondisciplinary reason is presumed to be COVID-19-related unless the employer proves otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Building service” means janitorial, building maintenance, or security services."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(4) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "building service" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "“Enterprise” means a hotel, private club, event center, airport hospitality operation, airport service provider, or the provision of building service to office, retail, or other commercial buildings."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(7) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "enterprise" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "“Laid-off employee” means any employee who was employed by the employer for six months or more and whose most recent separation from active employment by the employer occurred on or after March 4, 2020, and was due to a reason related to the COVID-19 pandemic, including a public health directive, government shutdown order, lack of business, a reduction in force, or other economic, nondisciplinary reason due to the COVID-19 pandemic. There shall be a presumption that a separation due to a lack of business, reduction in force, or other economic, nondisciplinary reason is due to a reason related to the COVID-19 pandemic, unless the employer establishes otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(10) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "laid-off employee" definition and presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the "building service," "enterprise," and "laid-off employee" definitions from Labor Code Section 2810.8(a). The statute defines several other terms this document does not separately quote or address in depth -- including "airport," "airport hospitality operation," "airport service provider," "event center," "hotel," and "private club" -- each of which carries its own size or scope threshold (for example, a "hotel" must have 50 or more guest rooms, counted as of the hotel's opening or December 31, 2019, whichever is greater). An enterprise's coverage cannot be confirmed from this clause alone; it requires checking the enterprise against the statute's full definitional list.

THE WRITTEN OFFER DUTY AND THE ORDER OF PREFERENCE
Once a covered employer establishes a new position, the statute gives it five business days to offer that position, in writing, to its own laid-off employees before filling it from outside that pool. The offer must be delivered either by hand or to the employee's last known physical address, and also by email and text message to the extent the employer has that contact information. A laid-off employee is "qualified" for the position -- and therefore entitled to the offer -- if the employee held the same or similar position at the enterprise at the time of that employee's most recent layoff. Where more than one laid-off employee is entitled to preference for the same position, the statute resolves the competition by length of service: the employer must offer the position to the laid-off employee with the greatest length of service, measured from that employee's date of hire, at the enterprise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Within five business days of establishing a position, an employer shall offer its laid-off employees in writing, either by hand or to their last known physical address, and by email and text message to the extent the employer possesses such information, all job positions that become available after the effective date of this section for which the laid-off employees are qualified. A laid-off employee is qualified for a position if the employee held the same or similar position at the enterprise at the time of the employee’s most recent layoff with the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, five-business-day written offer duty and the same-or-similar-position qualification standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "The employer shall offer positions to laid-off employees in an order of preference subject to paragraph (1) and this paragraph. If more than one employee is entitled to preference for a position, the employer shall offer the position to the laid-off employee with the greatest length of service based on the employee’s date of hire for the enterprise."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(2) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, length-of-service order of preference (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text does not define what it means to "establish" a position -- the event that starts the five-business-day offer clock -- so this clause cannot state a precise, generally applicable rule for identifying that moment; it will depend on the employer's own hiring and budgeting practices. This clause also does not address subdivision (b)(6)'s extension of these same offer-and-preference duties to certain successor, reorganized, or relocated employers, which is covered in a separate clause of this document.

THE EMPLOYEE'S RESPONSE WINDOW AND CONDITIONAL OFFERS
A laid-off employee who receives an offer under the statute is entitled to at least five business days from the date of receipt to accept or decline it. The statute defines "business day" for this purpose as any day other than a Saturday, a Sunday, or an official state holiday. Because more than one laid-off employee can be entitled to preference for the same position before the order-of-preference rule sorts out who actually receives it, the statute allows an employer to make simultaneous, conditional offers of employment to multiple laid-off employees at once, with the final, binding offer conditioned on how the preference system described elsewhere in this document sorts out the competing claims.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A laid-off employee who is offered a position pursuant to this section shall be given at least five business days, from the date of receipt, in which to accept or decline the offer. A “business day” is any day except Saturday, Sunday, or any official state holiday. An employer may make simultaneous, conditional offers of employment to laid-off employees, with a final offer of employment conditioned on application of the preference system set forth in paragraph (2)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(3) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, five-business-day response window, "business day" definition, and simultaneous conditional offers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  Known gap: The statute does not itself specify what happens to a conditional offer if the employee who would receive the final offer under the preference system has already responded, or how conditional offers interact with the separate five-business-day response window for the laid-off employee ultimately awarded the position -- this clause states the statutory mechanism as written without resolving that sequencing question.

RECORDKEEPING AND THE 30-DAY NOTICE WHEN RECALL IS DECLINED FOR LACK OF QUALIFICATIONS
The statute imposes its own three-year recordkeeping duty: for each laid-off employee, the employer must retain, for at least three years measured from the date of the written layoff notice, that employee's full legal name, job classification at separation, date of hire, last known address, last known email address, and last known telephone number, along with a copy of the written layoff notice and all records of communications with the employee about offers of employment made under the statute. Separately, if an employer declines to recall a laid-off employee on the grounds that the employee lacks qualifications and instead hires someone else, the statute requires the employer to give that laid-off employee written notice within 30 days, stating both the length of service of the person hired in the laid-off employee's place and all of the employer's reasons for the decision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employer must retain the following records for at least three years, measured from the date of the written notice regarding the layoff, for each laid-off employee: the employee’s full legal name; the employee’s job classification at the time of separation from employment; the employee’s date of hire; the employee’s last known address of residence; the employee’s last known email address; the employee’s last known telephone number; and a copy of the written notices regarding the layoff provided to the employee and all records of communications between the employer and the employee concerning offers of employment made to the employee pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(4) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, three-year recordkeeping duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "An employer that declines to recall a laid-off employee on the grounds of lack of qualifications and instead hires someone other than a laid-off employee shall provide the laid-off employee a written notice within 30 days including the length of service with the employer of those hired in lieu of that recall, along with all reasons for the decision."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(5) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, 30-day notice when declining recall for lack of qualifications (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  Known gap: Unlike the written offer duty in subdivision (b)(1), which specifies delivery by hand, mail, email, and text, the statute's text for this 30-day declined-recall notice does not itself specify a required delivery method -- this clause does not assume mail, email, hand delivery, or any other channel satisfies the duty, because the statute's own words do not say so for this particular notice.

COVERAGE DESPITE A CHANGE IN OWNERSHIP, FORM, ASSETS, OR LOCATION
The statute anticipates that a covered enterprise might change hands or shape after a COVID-19-related layoff, and it extends coverage to four such situations rather than letting them end the employer's obligations. The statute continues to apply where the ownership of the employer changed after the layoff but the enterprise still conducts the same or similar operations as it did before the COVID-19 state of emergency; where the employer's form of organization changed after the COVID-19 state of emergency; where another entity acquired substantially all of the employer's assets and conducts the same or similar operations using substantially the same assets; and where the employer relocated the operations at which the laid-off employee worked before the COVID-19 state of emergency to a different location. The statute's definition of "employer" is written to match: it expressly includes the successor employer described in these circumstances.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section also applies in any of the following circumstances:(A) The ownership of the employer changed after the separation from employment of a laid-off employee but the enterprise is conducting the same or similar operations as before the COVID-19 state of emergency.(B) The form of organization of the employer changed after the COVID-19 state of emergency.(C) Substantially all of the assets of the employer were acquired by another entity that conducts the same or similar operations using substantially the same assets.(D) The employer relocates the operations at which a laid-off employee was employed before the COVID-19 state of emergency to a different location."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(6) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, continued coverage after a change in ownership, form, assets, or location (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "“Employer” means any person, including a corporate officer or executive, who directly or indirectly or through an agent or any other person, including through the services of a temporary service or staffing agency or similar entity, owns or operates an enterprise and employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of any employee. “Employer” also means the successor employer as set forth under paragraph (6) of subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(6) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "employer" definition including the successor employer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (b)(6)'s four listed circumstances and the statute's own "employer" definition, but the statute does not further define "substantially all of the assets" or "same or similar operations" for purposes of this section, and this document did not locate published Division of Labor Standards Enforcement regulations interpreting those phrases under Section 2810.8 specifically (as distinct from the similarly worded but separate change-in-control test in California's grocery worker retention law, Labor Code §§ 2500-2522, covered elsewhere in this corpus).

ANTI-RETALIATION PROTECTION
The statute contains its own, separate anti-retaliation provision. An employer may not refuse to employ, terminate, reduce the compensation of, or otherwise take any adverse action against a laid-off employee for seeking to enforce rights under the statute, for participating in proceedings related to it, for opposing a practice the statute prohibits, or for otherwise asserting rights under it. That protection extends even to an employee or laid-off employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges that the statute was not followed -- the protection does not depend on the underlying allegation of noncompliance turning out to be correct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No employer shall refuse to employ, terminate, reduce in compensation, or otherwise take any adverse action against any laid-off employee as defined in subdivision (a) for seeking to enforce their rights under this section, for participating in proceedings related to this section, opposing any practice proscribed by this section, or otherwise asserting rights under this section. This subdivision shall also apply to any employee or laid-off employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges noncompliance with this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, anti-retaliation provision and good-faith mistaken-allegation protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  Known gap: The statute's text does not itself define "adverse action" for purposes of this anti-retaliation provision. This clause does not rely on case law to fill that gap: CourtListener's daily case-law search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no California court decision interpreting "adverse action" under this specific provision, Labor Code Section 2810.8(c), could be located or cited here.

ENFORCEMENT THROUGH THE LABOR COMMISSIONER: REMEDIES AND PENALTIES
Unlike some other California worker-protection statutes that allow a private lawsuit, this statute channels enforcement exclusively through the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (the Labor Commissioner's office): the statute gives that Division exclusive jurisdiction to enforce it, and states that the section may be enforced only through the procedures it sets out. A laid-off employee may file a complaint with the Division, which may award hiring and reinstatement rights; frontpay or backpay for each day a violation continues, calculated at not less than the highest of three specified rates (the employee's average regular rate over the employee's last three years in the same occupational classification, the employee's most recent regular rate with the employer, or the regular rate paid to whoever was employed in the position instead of the laid-off employee); and the value of benefits the employee would have received under the employer's benefit plan. The statute imposes no criminal penalties. A civil violation instead exposes the employer, or any agent or other person who violates or causes a violation, to a civil penalty of $100 per affected employee, plus liquidated damages of $500 per employee for each day the violation continues until cured -- both of which the Labor Commissioner recovers, deposits into the Labor and Workforce Development Fund, and pays to the employee as compensatory damages.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement shall have exclusive jurisdiction to enforce this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(d) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, exclusive enforcement jurisdiction of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "A laid-off employee may file a complaint with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement for violations of this section and may be awarded any or all of the following, as appropriate:(A) Hiring and reinstatement rights pursuant to this section.(B) Frontpay or backpay for each day during which the violation continues, which shall be calculated at a rate of compensation not less than the highest of any of the following rates:(i) The average regular rate of pay received by the laid-off employee during the last three years of that employee’s employment in the same occupation classification.(ii) The most recent regular rate received by the laid-off employee while employed by the employer.(iii) The regular rate received by an employee occupying the position in place of the laid-off employee that should have been employed.(C) Value of the benefits the laid-off employee would have received under the employer’s benefit plan."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(d)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, complaint process and recoverable remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "No criminal penalties shall be imposed for violation of this section.(3) Any employer, agent of the employer, or other person who violates or causes to be violated the provisions of this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of one hundred dollars ($100) for each employee whose rights under these provisions are violated and an additional sum payable as liquidated damages in the amount of five hundred dollars ($500), per employee, for each day the rights of an employee under this section are violated and continuing until such time as the violation is cured, which shall be recovered by the Labor Commissioner, deposited into the Labor and Workforce Development Fund, and paid to the employee as compensatory damages."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(d)(2)-(3) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, no criminal penalties and the civil penalty / liquidated damages scheme (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  Known gap: This clause does not quote or address subdivision (d)(4) through (d)(7), which describe the Labor Commissioner's investigative and citation procedures (cross-referencing Labor Code Sections 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, and 1197.1), the court's authority to grant injunctive relief, the interest rate applied to unpaid amounts (tied to Civil Code Section 3289(b)), and the statute's cumulative-remedies clause; nor does it address subdivision (e), which gives the Division authority to issue implementing regulations, determinations, and interpretations that themselves carry the force of law. None of those cross-referenced provisions were independently fetched or verified for this document.

COLLECTIVE BARGAINING, LOCAL ORDINANCES, AND THE STATUTE'S OWN SUNSET DATE
This statute sits alongside, rather than displacing, several other sources of law. It does not stop a local government from enacting its own ordinance that imposes greater standards, or additional enforcement mechanisms, than the state statute provides, and it does not limit a discharged or eligible employee's separate right to bring a common-law wrongful-termination claim. It can, however, be waived by a valid collective bargaining agreement -- but only where the waiver is explicit and stated in clear and unambiguous terms; an employer's unilateral implementation of terms and conditions of employment in a collective bargaining relationship does not count as a waiver. Finally, the statute carries its own expiration date, written into its own text: as most recently amended, it remains operative only until January 1, 2027, though a violation occurring on or before December 31, 2026 remains enforceable under the statute's enforcement procedures even after that date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Nothing in this section shall prohibit a local governmental agency from enacting ordinances that impose greater standards than, or establish additional enforcement provisions to, those prescribed by this section. This section shall not be construed to limit a discharged employee or eligible employee’s right to bring a common law cause of action for wrongful termination."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(f) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, local ordinances and preserved common-law wrongful termination claims (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "All of the provisions of this section, or any part of this section, may be waived in a valid collective bargaining agreement, but only if the waiver is explicitly set forth in that agreement in clear and unambiguous terms. Unilateral implementation of terms and conditions of employment by either party to a collective bargaining relationship shall not constitute or be permitted as a waiver of all or any part of the provisions of this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(g) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, collective bargaining waiver requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "(1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), this section shall remain operative only until January 1, 2027.(2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a violation of this section occurring on or before December 31, 2026, shall continue to be enforceable pursuant to subdivision (d)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(i) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, January 1, 2027 sunset date and continued enforceability of earlier violations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  "(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 280, Sec. 1. (AB 858) Effective January 1, 2026. Inoperative January 1, 2027, by its own provisions.)"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8, amendment history line (California Legislative Information, official text), California Legislative Information, amendment history confirming the current text's effective and inoperative dates (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.8.)
  Known gap: The January 1, 2027 sunset date reflects the statute's current text as amended by Assembly Bill 858 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 280, Sec. 1), effective January 1, 2026 and confirmed by leginfo.legislature.ca.gov's own amendment history line for this section; this document did not independently trace the statute's prior sunset dates or amendment history beyond that single history line. Because the statute is written to lapse absent further legislative action, whether it remains operative past January 1, 2027 depends on a future amendment that this document cannot anticipate; anyone relying on this document after that date should confirm the section's then-current status directly at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov before assuming it is still in force.

CERTIFICATION
The undersigned, Jordan Lee, certifies that the information above regarding the recall offer to Taylor Morgan accurately describes, to the best of the undersigned's knowledge, Bayview Grand Hotel, LLC's actions under California Labor Code Section 2810.8 as of the date signed below.

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: September 6, 2026

Jordan Lee
On behalf of Bayview Grand Hotel, LLC
San Diego, California

An employer may make simultaneous, conditional offers of employment to laid-off employees, with a final offer of employment conditioned on application of the preference system set forth in paragraph (2).

expectedJSON.gap: The statute does not itself specify what happens to a conditional offer if the employee who would receive the final offer under the preference system has already responded, or how conditional offers interact with the separate five-business-day response window for the laid-off employee ultimately awarded the position -- this clause states the statutory mechanism as written without resolving that sequencing question.

expectedJSON.body: The statute imposes its own three-year recordkeeping duty: for each laid-off employee, the employer must retain, for at least three years measured from the date of the written layoff notice, that employee's full legal name, job classification at separation, date of hire, last known address, last known email address, and last known telephone number, along with a copy of the written layoff notice and all records of communications with the employee about offers of employment made under the statute. Separately, if an employer declines to recall a laid-off employee on the grounds that the employee lacks qualifications and instead hires someone else, the statute requires the employer to give that laid-off employee written notice within 30 days, stating both the length of service of the person hired in the laid-off employee's place and all of the employer's reasons for the decision.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(4) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, three-year recordkeeping duty
citations.quote: An employer must retain the following records for at least three years, measured from the date of the written notice regarding the layoff, for each laid-off employee: the employee’s full legal name; the employee’s job classification at the time of separation from employment; the employee’s date of hire; the employee’s last known address of residence; the employee’s last known email address; the employee’s last known telephone number; and a copy of the written notices regarding the layoff provided to the employee and all records of communications between the employer and the employee concerning offers of employment made to the employee pursuant to this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(5) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, 30-day notice when declining recall for lack of qualifications
citations.quote: An employer that declines to recall a laid-off employee on the grounds of lack of qualifications and instead hires someone other than a laid-off employee shall provide the laid-off employee a written notice within 30 days including the length of service with the employer of those hired in lieu of that recall, along with all reasons for the decision.

expectedJSON.gap: Unlike the written offer duty in subdivision (b)(1), which specifies delivery by hand, mail, email, and text, the statute's text for this 30-day declined-recall notice does not itself specify a required delivery method -- this clause does not assume mail, email, hand delivery, or any other channel satisfies the duty, because the statute's own words do not say so for this particular notice.

expectedJSON.body: The statute anticipates that a covered enterprise might change hands or shape after a COVID-19-related layoff, and it extends coverage to four such situations rather than letting them end the employer's obligations. The statute continues to apply where the ownership of the employer changed after the layoff but the enterprise still conducts the same or similar operations as it did before the COVID-19 state of emergency; where the employer's form of organization changed after the COVID-19 state of emergency; where another entity acquired substantially all of the employer's assets and conducts the same or similar operations using substantially the same assets; and where the employer relocated the operations at which the laid-off employee worked before the COVID-19 state of emergency to a different location. The statute's definition of "employer" is written to match: it expressly includes the successor employer described in these circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(6) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, continued coverage after a change in ownership, form, assets, or location
citations.quote: This section also applies in any of the following circumstances:(A) The ownership of the employer changed after the separation from employment of a laid-off employee but the enterprise is conducting the same or similar operations as before the COVID-19 state of emergency.(B) The form of organization of the employer changed after the COVID-19 state of emergency.(C) Substantially all of the assets of the employer were acquired by another entity that conducts the same or similar operations using substantially the same assets.(D) The employer relocates the operations at which a laid-off employee was employed before the COVID-19 state of emergency to a different location.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(6) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "employer" definition including the successor employer
citations.quote: “Employer” means any person, including a corporate officer or executive, who directly or indirectly or through an agent or any other person, including through the services of a temporary service or staffing agency or similar entity, owns or operates an enterprise and employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of any employee. “Employer” also means the successor employer as set forth under paragraph (6) of subdivision (b).

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (b)(6)'s four listed circumstances and the statute's own "employer" definition, but the statute does not further define "substantially all of the assets" or "same or similar operations" for purposes of this section, and this document did not locate published Division of Labor Standards Enforcement regulations interpreting those phrases under Section 2810.8 specifically (as distinct from the similarly worded but separate change-in-control test in California's grocery worker retention law, Labor Code §§ 2500-2522, covered elsewhere in this corpus).

expectedJSON.body: The statute contains its own, separate anti-retaliation provision. An employer may not refuse to employ, terminate, reduce the compensation of, or otherwise take any adverse action against a laid-off employee for seeking to enforce rights under the statute, for participating in proceedings related to it, for opposing a practice the statute prohibits, or for otherwise asserting rights under it. That protection extends even to an employee or laid-off employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges that the statute was not followed -- the protection does not depend on the underlying allegation of noncompliance turning out to be correct.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(c) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, anti-retaliation provision and good-faith mistaken-allegation protection
citations.quote: No employer shall refuse to employ, terminate, reduce in compensation, or otherwise take any adverse action against any laid-off employee as defined in subdivision (a) for seeking to enforce their rights under this section, for participating in proceedings related to this section, opposing any practice proscribed by this section, or otherwise asserting rights under this section. This subdivision shall also apply to any employee or laid-off employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges noncompliance with this section.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute's text does not itself define "adverse action" for purposes of this anti-retaliation provision. This clause does not rely on case law to fill that gap: CourtListener's daily case-law search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no California court decision interpreting "adverse action" under this specific provision, Labor Code Section 2810.8(c), could be located or cited here.

expectedJSON.body: Unlike some other California worker-protection statutes that allow a private lawsuit, this statute channels enforcement exclusively through the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (the Labor Commissioner's office): the statute gives that Division exclusive jurisdiction to enforce it, and states that the section may be enforced only through the procedures it sets out. A laid-off employee may file a complaint with the Division, which may award hiring and reinstatement rights; frontpay or backpay for each day a violation continues, calculated at not less than the highest of three specified rates (the employee's average regular rate over the employee's last three years in the same occupational classification, the employee's most recent regular rate with the employer, or the regular rate paid to whoever was employed in the position instead of the laid-off employee); and the value of benefits the employee would have received under the employer's benefit plan. The statute imposes no criminal penalties. A civil violation instead exposes the employer, or any agent or other person who violates or causes a violation, to a civil penalty of $100 per affected employee, plus liquidated damages of $500 per employee for each day the violation continues until cured -- both of which the Labor Commissioner recovers, deposits into the Labor and Workforce Development Fund, and pays to the employee as compensatory damages.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(d) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, exclusive enforcement jurisdiction of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement
citations.quote: The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement shall have exclusive jurisdiction to enforce this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(d)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, complaint process and recoverable remedies
citations.quote: A laid-off employee may file a complaint with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement for violations of this section and may be awarded any or all of the following, as appropriate:(A) Hiring and reinstatement rights pursuant to this section.(B) Frontpay or backpay for each day during which the violation continues, which shall be calculated at a rate of compensation not less than the highest of any of the following rates:(i) The average regular rate of pay received by the laid-off employee during the last three years of that employee’s employment in the same occupation classification.(ii) The most recent regular rate received by the laid-off employee while employed by the employer.(iii) The regular rate received by an employee occupying the position in place of the laid-off employee that should have been employed.(C) Value of the benefits the laid-off employee would have received under the employer’s benefit plan.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(d)(2)-(3) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, no criminal penalties and the civil penalty / liquidated damages scheme
citations.quote: No criminal penalties shall be imposed for violation of this section.(3) Any employer, agent of the employer, or other person who violates or causes to be violated the provisions of this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of one hundred dollars ($100) for each employee whose rights under these provisions are violated and an additional sum payable as liquidated damages in the amount of five hundred dollars ($500), per employee, for each day the rights of an employee under this section are violated and continuing until such time as the violation is cured, which shall be recovered by the Labor Commissioner, deposited into the Labor and Workforce Development Fund, and paid to the employee as compensatory damages.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not quote or address subdivision (d)(4) through (d)(7), which describe the Labor Commissioner's investigative and citation procedures (cross-referencing Labor Code Sections 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, and 1197.1), the court's authority to grant injunctive relief, the interest rate applied to unpaid amounts (tied to Civil Code Section 3289(b)), and the statute's cumulative-remedies clause; nor does it address subdivision (e), which gives the Division authority to issue implementing regulations, determinations, and interpretations that themselves carry the force of law. None of those cross-referenced provisions were independently fetched or verified for this document.

expectedJSON.body: This statute sits alongside, rather than displacing, several other sources of law. It does not stop a local government from enacting its own ordinance that imposes greater standards, or additional enforcement mechanisms, than the state statute provides, and it does not limit a discharged or eligible employee's separate right to bring a common-law wrongful-termination claim. It can, however, be waived by a valid collective bargaining agreement -- but only where the waiver is explicit and stated in clear and unambiguous terms; an employer's unilateral implementation of terms and conditions of employment in a collective bargaining relationship does not count as a waiver. Finally, the statute carries its own expiration date, written into its own text: as most recently amended, it remains operative only until January 1, 2027, though a violation occurring on or before December 31, 2026 remains enforceable under the statute's enforcement procedures even after that date.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(f) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, local ordinances and preserved common-law wrongful termination claims
citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall prohibit a local governmental agency from enacting ordinances that impose greater standards than, or establish additional enforcement provisions to, those prescribed by this section. This section shall not be construed to limit a discharged employee or eligible employee’s right to bring a common law cause of action for wrongful termination.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(g) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, collective bargaining waiver requirements
citations.quote: All of the provisions of this section, or any part of this section, may be waived in a valid collective bargaining agreement, but only if the waiver is explicitly set forth in that agreement in clear and unambiguous terms. Unilateral implementation of terms and conditions of employment by either party to a collective bargaining relationship shall not constitute or be permitted as a waiver of all or any part of the provisions of this section.

citations.quote: (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), this section shall remain operative only until January 1, 2027.(2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a violation of this section occurring on or before December 31, 2026, shall continue to be enforceable pursuant to subdivision (d).

Because the statute is written to lapse absent further legislative action, whether it remains operative past January 1, 2027 depends on a future amendment that this document cannot anticipate; anyone relying on this document after that date should confirm the section's then-current status directly at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov before assuming it is still in force.
